course.title: Threat Intelligence Fundamentals
course.description: A research-driven, practice-oriented course that teaches how to collect, evaluate, analyze, structure, share, operationalize, and measure cyber threat intelligence. Learners progress from intelligence requirements and source evaluation through indicators, TTPs, STIX/TAXII, analytic hypotheses, attribution caution, vulnerability/exploit intelligence, dissemination, automation safety, and a defensive CTI fusion capstone.
prerequisites: Familiarity with security logs, IP addresses, domains, and common cybersecurity terminology.
A willingness to work only with data and systems that are authorized for training or operational use.
learningOutcomes: Write decision-focused intelligence requirements and map them to collection plans.
Evaluate threat-intelligence sources for provenance, reliability, relevance, timeliness, and bias.
Interpret indicators and TTPs without treating an observable as proof of maliciousness.
Use MITRE ATT&CK terminology to describe adversary behavior and support detection reasoning.
Explain STIX 2.1 and TAXII 2.1 roles in structured CTI representation and exchange.
Build evidence-based analytic hypotheses and communicate confidence and uncertainty.
Assess vulnerability intelligence with CVSS, EPSS, CISA KEV, asset criticality, and exposure context.
Produce concise intelligence products tailored to security consumers and operational decisions.
Design safer CTI automation pipelines with validation, provenance, quarantine, deduplication, scoring, and rollback.
Complete a defensive CTI fusion project with tests, traceable evidence, and explainable prioritization.

modules.title: Threat Intelligence Foundations
modules.description: Build a precise mental model of cyber threat intelligence, its consumers, and how it differs from raw data, indicators, and general security monitoring.

lessons.title: What Cyber Threat Intelligence Is
lessons.description: Define CTI as analyzed information that helps decision-makers understand and act on cyber threats.
learningObjectives: Define cyber threat intelligence, threat information, intelligence requirements, and consumers.
Distinguish raw observations from analyzed intelligence.
Explain why intelligence must be tied to decisions or actions.

notes.text: NIST describes cyber threat information broadly enough to include indicators, adversary TTPs, defensive recommendations, and incident-analysis findings. Intelligence adds context, interpretation, and relevance for a consumer.

items: Strategic intelligence supports leadership and risk decisions.
Operational intelligence supports campaigns, incidents, and planning.
Tactical intelligence focuses on adversary behaviors and detection implications.
Technical intelligence often deals with machine-usable artifacts such as domains, hashes, URLs, and IP addresses.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes intelligence from a raw indicator?
options: An indicator is already a complete risk decision.
Intelligence adds context and analysis so a consumer can make or support a decision.
Indicators are never useful for detection.
quiz.answer: Intelligence adds context and analysis so a consumer can make or support a decision.
quiz.explanation: A raw indicator is an observable artifact; intelligence adds context, confidence, relevance, and implications.

summary: CTI is decision-support information, not just a feed of observables.
Useful intelligence is contextual, timely, and relevant to a specific consumer.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Intelligence Requirements and the Intelligence Cycle
lessons.description: Turn business and security questions into explicit intelligence requirements and measurable collection needs.
learningObjectives: Write a primary intelligence requirement and supporting questions.
Separate what must be known from how it will be collected.
Explain the iterative cycle of requirements, collection, processing, analysis, production, dissemination, and feedback.

notes.text: A useful intelligence requirement states the decision-relevant question, not a preferred source or tool. The lifecycle is iterative: feedback can change requirements and collection priorities.

items: Requirements should have an owner and intended consumer.
Collection should be proportional to the question being answered.
Feedback is necessary to prevent intelligence from becoming a one-way feed.

practicals.title: Build an Intelligence Requirement Matrix
practicals.description: Turn three decision questions into a collection matrix with consumer, priority, source class, cadence, and explicit gaps.
steps: Write three decision-focused intelligence requirements for a fictional organization.
Assign a consumer and decision for each requirement.
Select at least two source classes per requirement.
Record collection cadence and one known limitation for each source.
Identify one gap and a fallback collection path for each requirement.
practicals.solution:
Example solution:
RQ1: Which identity threats should influence MFA investment? Consumer: security leadership. Sources: internal authentication telemetry + government/sector reporting. Gap: limited external visibility.
RQ2: Which behaviors are active in the current phishing campaign? Consumer: incident response. Sources: email telemetry + incident artifacts. Gap: unknown external infrastructure.
RQ3: Which TTPs should become endpoint detections? Consumer: detection engineering. Sources: internal endpoint telemetry + ATT&CK behavioral references. Gap: weak process telemetry.
practicals.output: A requirement-to-source matrix where every requirement has a consumer, decision, sources, cadence, limitation, and documented gap.

quiz.question: Which is the best intelligence requirement?
options: Which threat behaviors are most relevant to our internet-facing identity infrastructure this quarter?
quiz.answer: Which threat behaviors are most relevant to our internet-facing identity infrastructure this quarter?
quiz.explanation: It is a decision-relevant question with a defined scope and time period.

summary: Start from decisions and questions, then select sources.
Requirements should be revisited as the environment and threat landscape change.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Intelligence Types and Their Consumers
lessons.description: Choose intelligence products based on audience, time horizon, and decision impact.
learningObjectives: Compare strategic, operational, tactical, and technical intelligence.
Map a consumer to an appropriate product type.
Explain why the same underlying event may need different presentations for different audiences.

items: Executives need implications, trends, risk, and decisions.
Incident responders need campaign context, scope, and investigative leads.
Detection engineers need behaviors, telemetry requirements, and testable hypotheses.
Security tooling may consume normalized machine-readable observables.

quiz.question: Which consumer is most likely to need a strategic intelligence product?
options: A SOC analyst triaging one alert
An executive deciding whether to fund additional identity controls
A firewall administrator adding one temporary block
A malware sandbox engineer inspecting one sample
quiz.answer: An executive deciding whether to fund additional identity controls
quiz.explanation: Strategic intelligence is designed for higher-level decisions about risk and priorities.

summary: Intelligence is shaped by the consumer.
A technically accurate product can still fail if it is delivered in the wrong form.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Confidence, Relevance, Timeliness, and Uncertainty
lessons.description: Use structured confidence and caveats instead of overstating incomplete evidence.
learningObjectives: Explain confidence, relevance, timeliness, and source quality.
Write uncertainty statements that distinguish fact from inference.
Avoid false precision in assessments.

notes.text: Confidence should reflect the quality and quantity of evidence, not analyst enthusiasm. A good product explicitly identifies what is known, inferred, disputed, and unknown.

items: Source reliability and claim confidence are related but not identical.
Stale information can lose operational value even if it remains factually correct.
Confidence can be updated as corroborating or contradictory evidence appears.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to communicate an uncertain attribution assessment?
options: State the suspected actor as a proven fact.
State the assessment, supporting evidence, confidence, and what evidence would change the assessment.
Use a high severity label instead.
quiz.answer: State the assessment, supporting evidence, confidence, and what evidence would change the assessment.
quiz.explanation: This preserves analytical value without overstating evidence.

summary: Good intelligence makes uncertainty visible.
Confidence statements should be tied to evidence and revisited when evidence changes.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

tasks.title: Write Three Intelligence Requirements
tasks.description: Create three intelligence requirements for a fictional mid-sized organization.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce one strategic, one operational, and one technical requirement, each tied to a named consumer and a decision.
objectives: Write decision-focused questions.
Assign an intended consumer and time horizon.
List two supporting questions for each requirement.
requirements: Avoid requirements such as “collect threat feeds.” Start with a decision the consumer needs to make.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: Requirement 1: Which threat trends create the greatest identity risk over the next two quarters? Consumer: security leadership.
Requirement 2: Which attacker behaviors are associated with the ongoing phishing campaign? Consumer: incident response lead.
Requirement 3: Which observable behaviors should be converted into endpoint detections? Consumer: detection engineering.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task demonstrates that collection starts with an information need, and that the same environment may generate different requirements for different consumers.

modules.title: Collection, Sources, and Source Evaluation
modules.description: Build a disciplined collection strategy across public, commercial, internal, and partner sources while evaluating source quality and bias.

lessons.title: Threat Intelligence Sources
lessons.description: Survey open-source, internal telemetry, vendor, government, partner, and community sources.
learningObjectives: Classify intelligence sources by provenance.
Match source types to intelligence requirements.
Identify access, licensing, reliability, and coverage constraints.

items: Internal sources often provide the strongest environment-specific relevance.
Government and sector-sharing sources may add broader campaigns and warnings.
Commercial reporting can provide specialist analysis but may have product or collection biases.
Community sources can be useful but need stronger validation.

quiz.question: Which source is usually most directly relevant to a specific organization’s environment?
quiz.answer: Internal incident and telemetry data
quiz.explanation: Internal evidence directly reflects the organization’s assets, activity, and controls.

summary: Source diversity reduces blind spots.
No source should be trusted without considering provenance, collection method, scope, and incentives.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Source Reliability and Analytic Bias
lessons.description: Evaluate sources and recognize collection and reporting biases.
learningObjectives: Differentiate source reliability from claim confidence.
Identify confirmation, availability, and anchoring biases.
Document contradictory evidence rather than forcing consensus.

notes.text: A highly reputable publisher can still publish a claim that is wrong, incomplete, or outside the publisher’s normal expertise. Analysts should score or narrate both source reliability and confidence in the specific claim.

items: Search results are not evidence quality ratings.
Multiple copies of the same report are not independent corroboration.
Contradictory evidence should be preserved and analyzed, not silently discarded.

quiz.question: Why are five websites repeating the same sentence not necessarily five independent sources?
options: They may all derive the statement from the same original report
quiz.answer: They may all derive the statement from the same original report
quiz.explanation: Common-source repetition is not independent corroboration.

summary: Evaluate provenance, not just volume of reporting.
Analysts should actively seek disconfirming evidence for important claims.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Collection Planning and Source Gaps
lessons.description: Turn requirements into a collection plan with explicit gaps and priorities.
learningObjectives: Create a source-to-question mapping.
Identify collection gaps and fallback sources.
Set collection cadence based on decision urgency.

notes.text:
Requirement -> Source -> Collection cadence -> Gap -> Fallback
RQ-01 -> internal identity telemetry -> daily -> limited partner visibility -> sector-sharing source
Collection plans are living artifacts. When one source becomes unavailable, the plan should show which requirement is affected and what alternative evidence can reduce the gap.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a collection gap statement?
options: To make uncertainty and missing evidence explicit so decisions can account for it
quiz.answer: To make uncertainty and missing evidence explicit so decisions can account for it
quiz.explanation: A gap statement records what cannot currently be known or collected reliably.

summary: Collection should be requirement-driven.
A documented gap is more useful than an unspoken assumption.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Legal, Privacy, and Handling Considerations
lessons.description: Introduce safe handling, licensing, privacy, and dissemination constraints for CTI.
learningObjectives: Identify common handling concerns for intelligence data.
Explain why collection authority and sharing rules matter.
Describe the difference between technical utility and permission to collect or share.

notes.text: Threat intelligence may contain personal data, internal identifiers, or information subject to contracts and sharing restrictions. Handling requirements depend on law, policy, agreements, and context.
Use only data you are authorized to collect, store, analyze, and share. A technically useful source may still be impermissible for a particular use.

quiz.question: What should an analyst do before importing a third-party intelligence dataset into a production system?
options: Check authorization, licensing, privacy, handling, and integration requirements
quiz.answer: Check authorization, licensing, privacy, handling, and integration requirements
quiz.explanation: Operational use requires both technical suitability and appropriate permissions/handling.

summary: Handling constraints are part of intelligence quality.
Do not assume that availability on the internet implies unrestricted reuse.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

tasks.title: Build a Collection Plan
tasks.description: Map four intelligence requirements to appropriate sources and collection cadences.
tasks.problemStatement: For each requirement, identify at least two sources, their strengths, one gap, and a fallback source.
objectives: Create a requirement-to-source matrix.
Document at least one likely bias or coverage limitation per source.
Define a review cadence.
requirements: Use only source categories, not fabricated vendor claims.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: A strong plan uses different source classes where feasible and records what each source cannot answer.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task tests requirement-driven collection and gap management rather than feed accumulation.

modules.title: Indicators, Observables, and TTPs
modules.description: Learn how to work with technical observables without confusing an indicator with proof of maliciousness.

lessons.title: IOCs, Observables, and Context
lessons.description: Understand IPs, domains, URLs, hashes, file paths, certificates, email artifacts, and other observables.
learningObjectives: Define an IOC and a broader observable.
Explain why an observable needs context and provenance.
Identify common reasons an indicator may be benign or stale.

items: An IP address can represent shared hosting, cloud infrastructure, NAT, or a benign user.
A file hash identifies a specific byte sequence, not intent.
A domain may be legitimate infrastructure that was abused temporarily.
Context such as timestamp, role, campaign, and observed behavior changes interpretation.

quiz.question: Why is an IP address alone weak evidence of malicious activity?
options: An IP can be shared, reassigned, or legitimately used for many services
quiz.answer: An IP can be shared, reassigned, or legitimately used for many services
quiz.explanation: The same IP can have multiple legitimate or malicious contexts over time.

summary: Indicators are hypotheses or leads, not automatic proof.
Context and time are essential to interpretation.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures
lessons.description: Use TTPs to describe adversary behavior at a more durable level than individual indicators.
learningObjectives: Differentiate tactics, techniques, and procedures.
Explain why TTPs may remain useful when infrastructure changes.
Map observed behaviors to ATT&CK carefully.

notes.text: MITRE ATT&CK organizes adversary behavior into tactics and techniques. Tactics represent goals; techniques describe ways to achieve them. ATT&CK mappings support a shared language for analysis and detection engineering.

items: TTP analysis is generally more durable than a single IP or hash.
Technique mapping is evidence about behavior, not proof of attribution.

practicals.title: Enrich and Lifecycle Five Indicators
practicals.description: Create analyst-ready indicator records using context, provenance, confidence, sightings, and review/expiration metadata.
steps: Create five synthetic indicators using documentation-safe example domains/IPs or synthetic hashes.
Record source, first-seen, last-seen, confidence, related behavior, and intended use.
Add one enrichment field for each indicator such as hosting context, sighting, or related TTP.
Assign lifecycle state: new, validated, active, expired-review, or retired.
Write one sentence explaining why each indicator should or should not be promoted to an operational control.
practicals.solution: A correct solution keeps raw value, provenance, timing, and analyst judgment separate. High-confidence, recently sighted indicators with corroborating behavior can be considered for operational use; stale or weakly contextualized records remain investigative leads until validated.
practicals.output: Five complete indicator records with explicit provenance, confidence, lifecycle state, and an action recommendation.

quiz.question: In ATT&CK, a tactic represents:
quiz.answer: An adversary objective or goal
quiz.explanation: Tactics describe the why; techniques describe how.

summary: Behavioral intelligence can outlast infrastructure changes.
Map techniques from observed evidence, not from assumptions about the actor.

lessons.title: Indicator Enrichment and Pivoting
lessons.description: Learn a repeatable method for adding context to a technical indicator.
learningObjectives: Define enrichment fields such as passive DNS, ASN, WHOIS/RDAP, reputation, malware relationships, and sightings.
Prioritize pivots based on the intelligence question.
Track which enrichment results are facts versus derived assessments.

notes.text:
Indicator
  -> time context
  -> infrastructure context
  -> sightings
  -> related observables
  -> TTP/campaign context
  -> assessment
Enrichment should answer a question. Gathering every available field can create noise and analyst fatigue.

quiz.question: What is the best reason to enrich an indicator?
options: To add decision-relevant context that changes interpretation or action
quiz.answer: To add decision-relevant context that changes interpretation or action
quiz.explanation: Enrichment is valuable when it reduces uncertainty or supports a decision.

summary: Enrichment should be purposeful and provenance-aware.
Record when the enrichment was obtained because infrastructure and reputation change.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Indicator Lifecycle and Expiration
lessons.description: Manage indicator freshness, confidence, sighting history, and retirement.
learningObjectives: Explain why indicators need time-to-live or review logic.
Design lifecycle states such as new, validated, active, expired, and retired.
Avoid permanent blocking of stale infrastructure.

items: Indicators change meaning over time.
Expiration should depend on indicator type and collection context, not a universal timer.
Sighting history can justify renewed relevance.
Retired indicators should remain available for historical investigations where policy permits.

quiz.question: Why should many indicators have an expiration or review date?
options: Because their relevance and ownership can change over time
quiz.answer: Because their relevance and ownership can change over time
quiz.explanation: Indicator usefulness and risk can change as infrastructure is reassigned or campaigns end.

summary: Indicator management is a lifecycle process.
Historical retention can remain useful even when operational blocking expires.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

tasks.title: Create an Indicator Enrichment Record
tasks.description: Take five fictional indicators and create analyst-ready records with context and lifecycle metadata.
tasks.problemStatement: For each indicator, record type, value, first seen, last seen, source, confidence, related behavior, disposition, and expiration/review date.
objectives: Separate raw value from analyst assessment.
Record provenance and timestamps.
Choose a defensible disposition.
requirements: Do not use real personal data or real credentials.
Use synthetic indicators such as example domains and documentation-safe IP ranges.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: A strong record makes it possible for another analyst to understand why the indicator matters and when it should be reconsidered.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task develops indicator hygiene and prevents uncontrolled IOC accumulation.

modules.title: STIX, TAXII, and Threat-Intel Data Modeling
modules.description: Learn standards-based threat-information representation and exchange.

lessons.title: STIX 2.1 Concepts
lessons.description: Understand STIX objects, relationships, bundles, and machine-readable CTI.
learningObjectives: Explain why STIX exists.
Identify common STIX object categories.
Describe relationships between observables, indicators, identities, malware, threat actors, and sightings.

notes.text: OASIS STIX 2.1 defines a language and serialization model for expressing cyber threat and observable information in a structured, machine-readable way.

items: STIX represents more than indicators; it can model relationships and context.
A STIX object should preserve enough context for consumers to understand the claim.

practicals.title: Inspect a STIX 2.1 Indicator Bundle
practicals.description: Read a small STIX bundle and explain what is represented, what is observed, and what remains an analyst assessment.
steps: Create a minimal STIX 2.1 bundle containing one indicator object, one identity object, and one relationship.
Read the object types and identifiers without assuming that the indicator is malicious in your environment.
Record which fields establish provenance and validity dates.
Explain how a sighting would add local operational evidence.
practicals.solution: A correct analysis identifies the STIX object types, preserves object IDs and timestamps, distinguishes the indicator pattern from a local sighting, and states that schema validity does not prove the underlying claim is true.
practicals.output: A short interpretation that maps each object to its role and clearly separates structured representation from analyst conclusions.

quiz.question: What is a primary advantage of STIX?
options: It is a faster network protocol
It provides a structured language for representing CTI consistently and machine-readably
quiz.answer: It provides a structured language for representing CTI consistently and machine-readably
quiz.explanation: STIX is a structured language/format for CTI exchange.

summary: Structured CTI improves interoperability.
The schema does not guarantee that the content itself is accurate.

resources.title: OASIS Cyber Threat Intelligence Technical Committee

lessons.title: STIX Indicators, Observed Data, and Sightings
lessons.description: Distinguish a rule-like indicator from observed activity and sightings.
learningObjectives: Explain the conceptual difference between indicator content and observations.
Describe why sightings add valuable operational context.
Avoid treating an indicator object as proof that activity occurred in your environment.

items: An indicator expresses a pattern or observable associated with a condition.
Observed data describes data that was actually observed.
Sightings communicate that an entity or indicator was observed or used, depending on the modeled object and context.

quiz.question: Why are sightings valuable in CTI?
options: They show that an indicator or entity was observed, adding operational context
They eliminate the need for provenance
quiz.answer: They show that an indicator or entity was observed, adding operational context
quiz.explanation: Sightings provide evidence of observation and can improve relevance assessment.

summary: Separate predicted/associated indicators from observed activity.
Operational sightings can increase confidence and help prioritize response.

lessons.title: TAXII 2.1 and Automated Exchange
lessons.description: Understand how TAXII transports CTI between compatible producers and consumers.
learningObjectives: Explain the relationship between STIX and TAXII.
Describe collections, discovery, and client/server exchange at a high level.
Identify authentication, trust, and filtering concerns in automation.

notes.text: OASIS TAXII 2.1 defines an application-layer protocol for communicating cyber threat information, commonly carrying STIX content over RESTful APIs.

items: STIX defines how CTI is represented; TAXII defines how CTI is exchanged.
Automation needs trust, authentication, authorization, rate controls, and validation.

quiz.question: Which statement is correct?
options: STIX is the transport protocol and TAXII is the data model
STIX is the CTI language/model and TAXII is an exchange protocol
quiz.answer: STIX is the CTI language/model and TAXII is an exchange protocol
quiz.explanation: STIX represents information; TAXII transports it between systems.

summary: Interoperability has both data-model and transport components.
Automation must validate incoming data before using it operationally.

lessons.title: Data Quality, Normalization, and Validation
lessons.description: Prepare CTI for downstream use without silently altering meaning.
learningObjectives: Identify normalization issues in indicators and metadata.
Validate required fields before ingestion.
Preserve original source content or provenance where policy permits.

notes.text:
Validation checklist
- type and syntax
- source/provenance
- timestamp
- confidence
- expiration
- handling label
- duplicate status
Never normalize away information that changes interpretation, such as original timestamps, source identity, or caveats.

quiz.question: Why should original provenance be preserved when CTI is normalized?
options: So analysts can trace the normalized record back to its source and evaluate trust
quiz.answer: So analysts can trace the normalized record back to its source and evaluate trust
quiz.explanation: Traceability is required for later validation and investigation.

summary: Normalization should improve interoperability without destroying context.
Validation should include semantic and operational checks, not only syntax.

tasks.title: Design a STIX/TAXII Intake Checklist
tasks.description: Create a checklist for safely ingesting a new machine-readable CTI source.
tasks.problemStatement: The checklist must validate structure, provenance, handling, duplicates, freshness, confidence, and downstream actionability.
objectives: Include pre-ingestion and post-ingestion checks.
Define what causes a record to be quarantined.
Include a human-review path for ambiguous data.
requirements: The transport can succeed while the content is still untrustworthy or unsuitable.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: Quarantine malformed or policy-violating data rather than auto-promoting it to blocking controls.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task connects CTI standards to operational data-quality controls.

modules.title: Analysis, Attribution, and Campaign Assessment
modules.description: Develop disciplined analytical methods for linking evidence, campaigns, and actor hypotheses.

lessons.title: From Data to Analytic Hypothesis
lessons.description: Move from observables and reports to testable analytic questions.
learningObjectives: Separate observation, inference, hypothesis, and assessment.
Write an explicit analytic hypothesis.
Identify evidence that would confirm or disconfirm it.

notes.text: Observation -> hypothesis -> evidence needed -> competing explanation -> assessment -> confidence
The strongest analytical products make the reasoning path visible enough for another analyst to challenge it.

quiz.question: What makes an analytic hypothesis useful?
options: It states a claim that can be tested against available evidence and competing explanations
quiz.answer: It states a claim that can be tested against available evidence and competing explanations
quiz.explanation: Testability helps analysts avoid premature conclusions.

summary: Make reasoning explicit and challengeable.
Always consider at least one plausible alternative explanation for consequential claims.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Campaign and Cluster Analysis
lessons.description: Group related events or infrastructure using shared evidence without overfitting.
learningObjectives: Define clustering features such as timing, infrastructure, malware, TTPs, targeting, and language.
Explain why one shared feature is rarely enough for a strong cluster.
Document inclusion and exclusion criteria.

items: Clusters are analytical constructs, not necessarily named actor identities.
Shared infrastructure may reflect common hosting rather than common control.
Timing and behavioral consistency can strengthen a cluster when independently observed.

quiz.question: Which is strongest for campaign clustering?
options: Multiple independent features that align across incidents and time
quiz.answer: Multiple independent features that align across incidents and time
quiz.explanation: Converging independent evidence is more persuasive than one weak commonality.

summary: Clusters should have explicit criteria.
Avoid circular reasoning where the same report is used both to define and prove the cluster.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Attribution: Capabilities, Infrastructure, and Intent
lessons.description: Understand the limits of actor attribution and how evidence is layered.
learningObjectives: Differentiate capability, infrastructure, behavior, targeting, and intent.
Explain why attribution should be expressed probabilistically.
Identify common attribution traps.

notes.text: Attribution is a high-uncertainty analytical task. Do not convert tool or infrastructure overlap into identity without corroborating evidence.

items: Capability overlap is common because tools are reused or publicly available.
Infrastructure can be compromised or rented.
False flags and reused malware complicate attribution.

quiz.question: Which is the best practice for actor attribution?
options: Treat one malware family as proof of actor identity
State the attribution assessment with confidence and evidence, including alternatives
Use the loudest report as truth
quiz.answer: State the attribution assessment with confidence and evidence, including alternatives
quiz.explanation: Attribution should be evidence-based and uncertainty-aware.

summary: Attribution is an assessment, not a default label.
Analysts should explain what evidence is decisive and what remains ambiguous.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Threat Actor Profiles and Behavior Mapping
lessons.description: Build concise profiles that emphasize behaviors and operational relevance.
learningObjectives: Create a behavior-oriented actor profile.
Map reported behaviors to ATT&CK without confusing mapping with attribution.
Connect actor behaviors to detection and defensive implications.

notes.text: MITRE ATT&CK software and group pages document publicly reported behavior relationships. These entries represent reported associations rather than exhaustive or infallible coverage.

quiz.question: What should a useful actor profile emphasize?
options: Evidence-backed behaviors, targeting, capabilities, confidence, and defensive implications
quiz.answer: Evidence-backed behaviors, targeting, capabilities, confidence, and defensive implications
quiz.explanation: A useful profile supports action and keeps evidence visible.

summary: Behavior mapping is more operationally useful than labels alone.
Actor names and aliases can change; behavior remains central.

tasks.title: Produce an Attribution Assessment
tasks.description: Write an evidence-based assessment about two competing actor hypotheses using a fictional incident set.
tasks.problemStatement: Assess which hypothesis is better supported, list corroborating evidence, contradictory evidence, confidence, and what new collection would reduce uncertainty.
objectives: Use at least three independent evidence categories.
Include a competing explanation.
Do not claim certainty unless the scenario supports it.
requirements: Treat ATT&CK mapping as behavioral evidence, not automatic attribution.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: A defensible assessment might conclude “Hypothesis A is more consistent with the evidence” while explicitly preserving uncertainty.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task tests analytical tradecraft, competing hypotheses, and disciplined attribution language.

modules.title: Vulnerability and Exploit Intelligence
modules.description: Integrate vulnerability intelligence with threat context and asset criticality.

lessons.title: CVE, CWE, and Vulnerability Language
lessons.description: Understand common vulnerability identifiers and weakness taxonomies.
learningObjectives: Define CVE and CWE at a practical level.
Explain why a vulnerability identifier does not itself determine business risk.
Connect weakness classes to defensive analysis.

items: CVE identifiers track specific publicly known vulnerabilities.
CWE describes categories of software and design weaknesses.
Vulnerability records require affected-product, version, configuration, and remediation context.

quiz.question: What does CWE primarily describe?
options: A category of software or design weakness
quiz.answer: A category of software or design weakness
quiz.explanation: CWE organizes recurring weakness types.

summary: Identifiers improve communication but do not replace contextual assessment.
Use affected-version and deployment evidence before claiming exposure.

lessons.title: CVSS v4.0 and Severity
lessons.description: Interpret standardized vulnerability severity without treating it as a complete organizational risk score.
learningObjectives: Explain Base, Threat, Environmental, and Supplemental metric groups at a high level.
Use CVSS terminology accurately.
Distinguish standardized severity from business risk.

notes.text: CVSS provides standardized severity scoring. Environmental context can change how a vulnerability should be understood, while organizational prioritization should also consider asset criticality, exposure, exploitation evidence, and available mitigations.

quiz.question: Which CVSS metric group is intended to reflect characteristics specific to an organization’s deployment?
quiz.answer: Environmental
quiz.explanation: Environmental metrics are designed to adjust for deployment context.

summary: CVSS is a severity framework, not a universal remediation priority algorithm.
Combine CVSS with asset and threat context.

lessons.title: EPSS and Exploitation Likelihood
lessons.description: Use EPSS as probabilistic evidence about exploitation likelihood while recognizing its scope and limitations.
learningObjectives: Explain what an exploitation-probability estimate is.
Use EPSS alongside other risk signals.
Avoid interpreting probability as certainty of exploitation in a specific environment.

notes.text: EPSS estimates the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild over a defined time horizon, based on observed data and modeling. It is a predictive signal, not evidence that your organization is currently being exploited.

quiz.question: What is the best use of EPSS in vulnerability prioritization?
options: As proof that an asset is compromised
As one predictive signal about exploitation likelihood alongside exposure and asset context
As a replacement for patch testing
quiz.answer: As one predictive signal about exploitation likelihood alongside exposure and asset context
quiz.explanation: EPSS contributes probabilistic context; it is not a compromise detector.

summary: Probabilistic threat signals should be combined with local evidence.
Do not confuse population-level exploitation likelihood with local compromise evidence.

lessons.title: CISA KEV and Threat-Informed Prioritization
lessons.description: Use known-exploitation evidence to raise the priority of vulnerabilities that matter to defenders.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of the KEV catalog.
Use KEV status as one input to remediation prioritization.
Combine exploitation evidence with exposure, asset criticality, and mitigations.

notes.text: CISA describes the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as an authoritative source of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild and recommends using it as an input to vulnerability-management prioritization.

quiz.question: What does inclusion in CISA KEV primarily tell a defender?
options: The vulnerability is always critical in every environment
The vulnerability is known to have been exploited in the wild and should inform prioritization
quiz.answer: The vulnerability is known to have been exploited in the wild and should inform prioritization
quiz.explanation: KEV provides evidence of real-world exploitation, which can raise urgency.

summary: Exploit evidence can be decisive when combined with exposure and asset value.
KEV is not a substitute for local vulnerability validation.

tasks.title: Build a Threat-Informed Vulnerability Priority Model
tasks.description: Prioritize a fictional vulnerability backlog using severity, exploit evidence, exposure, and asset criticality.
tasks.problemStatement: Rank at least six vulnerabilities and justify the order with explicit evidence rather than CVSS alone.
objectives: Use CVSS, KEV/EPSS-style context, exposure, asset criticality, and compensating controls.
Document uncertainties.
Separate technical severity from organizational priority.
requirements: No real exploit code is required.
Use only scenario facts provided by the instructor or dataset.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: A lower CVSS item may outrank another when it is actively exploited and affects a critical internet-facing asset.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task develops risk-based prioritization and prevents score-only decision making.

modules.title: Sharing, Dissemination, and Operationalization
modules.description: Turn analyzed intelligence into actionable products and machine-consumable outputs while controlling dissemination risk.

lessons.title: Intelligence Production and Writing
lessons.description: Write concise intelligence that makes the assessment and implications easy to act on.
learningObjectives: Structure an intelligence report around the consumer’s decision.
Separate assessment, evidence, implications, and recommendations.
Write concise confidence and caveat statements.

notes.text:
Product structure
1. Executive assessment
2. Key evidence
3. Confidence / caveats
4. Operational implications
5. Recommended actions
6. Sources / provenance
The product should answer “so what?” and “what should we do next?” without hiding uncertainty.

practicals.title: Write a CTI-to-Action Brief
practicals.description: Convert a fictional threat report into a one-page operational brief for a SOC lead.
steps: State the assessment in one paragraph.
List three evidence items and their provenance.
State confidence and one important uncertainty.
Map one observed behavior to an ATT&CK technique where justified.
Recommend two defensive actions and one collection action that would reduce uncertainty.
practicals.solution: The brief should lead with the assessment, then evidence, confidence, operational implications, and actions. It should avoid unverified actor attribution and make clear which evidence is direct versus inferred.
practicals.output: A concise analyst-ready brief that supports a decision while preserving uncertainty and provenance.

quiz.question: Which section should make the analyst’s conclusion easiest to understand?
options: A clear assessment with evidence and implications
quiz.answer: A clear assessment with evidence and implications
quiz.explanation: Decision-makers need the conclusion and why it is supported.

summary: Good intelligence is written for a consumer, not for the analyst alone.
Evidence and confidence make the assessment auditable.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Dissemination and Handling Labels
lessons.description: Choose recipients and channels that match sensitivity, sharing agreements, and operational need.
learningObjectives: Explain need-to-know and least dissemination.
Identify handling restrictions that can affect onward sharing.
Document recipient scope and intended use.

notes.text: Dissemination should follow policy, agreements, law, and applicable handling markings. Never infer sharing permission solely from the fact that intelligence exists.

items: The smallest useful audience reduces accidental exposure.
Recipients should understand handling restrictions and whether redistribution is permitted.

quiz.question: Why is recipient scope part of intelligence production?
options: Because every report must be public
Because the sensitivity and permitted use of information can depend on who receives it
Because CTI has no privacy concerns
quiz.answer: Because the sensitivity and permitted use of information can depend on who receives it
quiz.explanation: Dissemination is a governance and risk decision.

summary: Need-to-know and handling controls are operational security controls.
Document sharing constraints explicitly.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Turning Intelligence into Detection Requirements
lessons.description: Translate CTI into telemetry, hypotheses, and testable detection logic.
learningObjectives: Convert a TTP or intelligence claim into observable behaviors.
Identify required telemetry and possible detection gaps.
Write a detection hypothesis that can be validated.

notes.text: CTI claim -> behavior -> observable -> telemetry source -> detection hypothesis -> validation plan

items: Intelligence should not become a block rule automatically.
A good detection requirement identifies the signal, context, and likely false-positive conditions.

quiz.question: What is the best first step when converting a TTP into a detection?
options: Block every IP associated with the TTP
Identify the observable behavior and required telemetry
quiz.answer: Identify the observable behavior and required telemetry
quiz.explanation: Detection engineering begins with observable behavior and visibility requirements.

summary: Threat intelligence becomes operational when it changes detection, prevention, prioritization, or investigation.
Every detection should have a validation plan.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Sharing Communities and Collaboration
lessons.description: Understand sector and community sharing as a way to improve collective defense.
learningObjectives: Explain benefits and risks of CTI sharing.
Identify why common formats and agreements matter.
Describe feedback loops between sharing communities and internal defenders.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-150 describes goals, sources, scope, rules, communities, and effective use of threat information sharing.

items: Sharing can increase visibility into threats that one organization would not see alone.
Participation requires governance, trust, handling rules, and useful contribution.

quiz.question: Why do common standards help CTI sharing?
options: They reduce friction in representing and exchanging information
They eliminate the need for human analysis
quiz.answer: They reduce friction in representing and exchanging information
quiz.explanation: Standards improve interoperability but do not guarantee content quality.

summary: Sharing is both a technical and governance problem.
Contribution quality influences community value.

tasks.title: Create an Intelligence-to-Action Brief
tasks.description: Turn a fictional campaign report into a one-page operational brief for defenders.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce a concise brief containing assessment, confidence, key evidence, impacted assets, detection implications, and recommended actions.
objectives: Tailor the product to a SOC lead audience.
Include at least two detection requirements.
State what remains unknown.
requirements: Do not prescribe unauthorized offensive action.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: Keep raw indicator detail in an appendix-like section and lead with decisions and implications.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task tests whether intelligence can be transformed into a usable operational product.

modules.title: Automation, Quality, and CTI Operations
modules.description: Learn practical automation patterns, feed hygiene, metrics, and lifecycle management.

lessons.title: Feed Ingestion Pipelines
lessons.description: Design a safe ingestion pipeline from source to downstream system.
learningObjectives: Describe stages of an automated CTI pipeline.
Identify validation, deduplication, enrichment, and quarantine controls.
Explain why downstream blocking should be decoupled from untrusted intake.

notes.text: Source -> intake -> schema validation -> provenance checks -> normalization -> deduplication -> enrichment -> scoring -> review/automation
Do not directly convert unvalidated third-party intelligence into high-impact controls. Use staged promotion and clear rollback paths.

quiz.question: Why should untrusted CTI pass through validation before affecting production controls?
options: Malformed, stale, or misleading data can cause operational harm
quiz.answer: Malformed, stale, or misleading data can cause operational harm
quiz.explanation: Staged validation reduces unintended impact.

summary: Automation should reduce repetitive work while preserving safety checks.
Quarantine and rollback are core operational controls.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Deduplication, Scoring, and Confidence Propagation
lessons.description: Keep CTI usable at scale by merging duplicates and preserving uncertainty.
learningObjectives: Define duplicate and near-duplicate indicators.
Design a scoring approach using source and context without implying certainty.
Propagate confidence cautiously when records are merged.

items: A single indicator may arrive from multiple sources.
Merging should preserve provenance and source-specific timestamps.
Scores should be explainable and recalculable as evidence changes.

quiz.question: What should happen to source provenance when duplicate indicators are merged?
options: Preserve the source lineage so the merged record remains auditable
Replace it with a guessed source
quiz.answer: Preserve the source lineage so the merged record remains auditable
quiz.explanation: Multiple-source provenance can explain why confidence increased or conflicted.

summary: Scoring should remain interpretable.
Never hide conflicting sources merely to simplify a record.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Metrics and Intelligence Effectiveness
lessons.description: Measure whether CTI improves outcomes, not just how many indicators are ingested.
learningObjectives: Distinguish activity metrics from outcome metrics.
Define useful CTI program measures.
Avoid vanity metrics that reward feed volume rather than value.

items: Activity metric: number of indicators ingested.
Quality metric: proportion of records with complete provenance and freshness.
Outcome metric: number of validated detections or remediation decisions improved by CTI.
Feedback metric: percentage of consumers who report that products answered their requirements.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest outcome metric for a CTI program?
options: Number of decisions or detections materially improved by intelligence
quiz.answer: Number of decisions or detections materially improved by intelligence
quiz.explanation: Outcome metrics connect intelligence work to defensive value.

summary: Measure usefulness, not volume.
Metrics should map back to requirements and consumers.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Operational Runbooks and Analyst Handoffs
lessons.description: Make CTI repeatable across analysts and shifts.
learningObjectives: Create a runbook for common CTI workflows.
Define inputs, outputs, escalation, and evidence requirements.
Design handoffs that preserve context and uncertainty.

notes.text: Runbooks reduce variation in repetitive workflows such as indicator triage, enrichment, watchlist review, and intelligence-product updates.

items: Every runbook should define exit conditions.
Handoffs should state what was checked, what remains unknown, and what next action is expected.

quiz.question: Why are explicit exit conditions useful in CTI runbooks?
options: They force analysts to stop regardless of evidence
They define when the workflow is complete or requires escalation
They remove the need for analysts
quiz.answer: They define when the workflow is complete or requires escalation
quiz.explanation: Clear exit conditions prevent both premature closure and endless analysis.

summary: Operational quality depends on repeatability and clear escalation.
Runbooks should be maintained as systems and threats change.

tasks.title: Design a Safe CTI Automation Pipeline
tasks.description: Design an architecture for automatically ingesting and scoring CTI before promotion to a defensive control.
tasks.problemStatement: Include validation, provenance, deduplication, confidence scoring, quarantine, human review, rollback, and monitoring.
objectives: Identify trust boundaries.
Define at least three failure modes and mitigations.
Separate ingestion from high-impact enforcement.
requirements: Use staged promotion instead of direct blocking.
tasks.hint: Document your reasoning and keep the evidence traceable.
solutionCode: A good solution uses intake and quarantine first, then promotion based on policy and confidence. It logs every transformation and supports rollback.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task combines CTI data quality with safe automation design.

modules.title: Final Project — Intelligence Fusion and Prioritization Desk
modules.description: Build a realistic defensive CTI workflow that fuses multiple source types into analyst-ready assessments and prioritized actions. The project is the final practical assessment and has no separate module tasks.

lessons.title: Capstone Requirements and Architecture
lessons.description: Define the final project’s data model, workflow, validation boundaries, and acceptance criteria.
learningObjectives: Design the project flow from requirements to collection, fusion, prioritization, and reporting.
Define acceptance criteria for traceability and safe automation.
Keep synthetic or openly licensed data in the lab.

notes.text: Requirement -> sources -> normalized events -> evidence links -> assessment -> priority -> product -> feedback
The capstone is intentionally defensive: it prioritizes intelligence and supports analyst decisions; it does not exploit systems or perform unauthorized actions.

quiz.question: What must remain traceable in the capstone?
options: The connection from output back to evidence and source provenance
quiz.answer: The connection from output back to evidence and source provenance
quiz.explanation: Traceability allows an analyst to review and challenge the result.

summary: The capstone is built around evidence lineage.
Safe automation requires explicit boundaries and explainable outputs.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-150 — Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing

lessons.title: Capstone Validation and Analyst Review
lessons.description: Validate the capstone with structured test cases, edge cases, and human review.
learningObjectives: Test malformed indicators, duplicates, stale data, and conflicting sources.
Verify that uncertainty is retained.
Evaluate whether outputs are useful to a security consumer.

notes.text: A passing software test suite does not prove an intelligence assessment is correct. Technical validation and analytical review are separate quality gates.

quiz.question: Which scenario is most important to test in a CTI fusion pipeline?
options: Conflicting, stale, malformed, duplicated, and high-impact inputs
quiz.answer: Conflicting, stale, malformed, duplicated, and high-impact inputs
quiz.explanation: These are common failure modes that can distort downstream decisions.

summary: Technical tests verify behavior; analyst review verifies meaning and usefulness.
The final assessment should preserve evidence and uncertainty.

project.name: Intelligence Fusion and Prioritization Desk
project.description: A defensive local tool that fuses synthetic threat-intelligence records, preserves provenance during deduplication, applies transparent prioritization rules, and emits an analyst-oriented report. It demonstrates requirements-driven CTI, indicator lifecycle, confidence, enrichment, vulnerability/threat context, safe automation, and operational reporting.
steps: Define the project data contract and trust boundaries.
Validate incoming records and reject malformed or policy-invalid data.
Normalize indicator fields while preserving source provenance and timestamps.
Deduplicate indicators while retaining all source lineage and the strongest relevant context.
Apply explainable prioritization rules using exploitation context, exposure, asset criticality, confidence, and behavioral context.
Generate a report that contains evidence, priority, reasons, and analyst notes.
Test normal input, duplicates, low-confidence records, high-priority records, and malformed confidence values.
Review the final report manually for analytical usefulness and uncertainty.

code.README.md:
# Intelligence Fusion and Prioritization Desk

A local defensive training project. It reads synthetic CTI records, normalizes fields,
deduplicates indicators, applies explainable prioritization rules, and emits an analyst report.

It does not scan networks, exploit systems, test credentials, or contact external targets.
code.test_cti_tool.py:
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

def test_cli_and_dedupe():
    p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(ROOT/'cti_tool.py'), str(ROOT/'sample_cti.json')], capture_output=True, text=True)
    assert p.returncode == 0, p.stderr
    report = json.loads(p.stdout)
    assert report['record_count'] == 4
    assert report['unique_indicator_count'] == 3
    assert report['records'][0]['priority'] in {'high','critical'}
    assert len(report['records'][0]['sources']) >= 1

def test_rejects_bad_confidence(tmp_path):
    bad = tmp_path/'bad.json'
    bad.write_text(json.dumps([{
        'id':'bad','indicator_type':'domain','value':'bad.example','source':'x','confidence':2,
        'first_seen':'2026-09-01T00:00:00Z','last_seen':'2026-09-01T00:01:00Z'
    }]), encoding='utf-8')
    p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(ROOT/'cti_tool.py'), str(bad)], capture_output=True, text=True)
    assert p.returncode != 0

project.explanation: The architecture separates intake from action. Incoming records are validated before normalization. Deduplication merges identical observable keys while keeping source lineage and selected contextual fields. Prioritization is intentionally transparent: each point has an explicit reason so analysts can challenge the output. The report does not claim that a priority score proves compromise or maliciousness; it is a triage aid. The tests cover both expected processing and invalid data. This mirrors a safe CTI program pattern where machine processing accelerates analysts but does not silently replace analytical judgment.
